- ✗ **A. Spot Instances:** Spot lowers the price of compute, not of third-party licenses, and it can be interrupted with a two-minute notice, which suits few database workloads.
- ✓ **B. Dedicated Hosts (correct):** the company gets a whole physical server with visible sockets and cores, so it can count and reuse its per-socket or per-core licenses and stay within the vendor's terms.
- ✗ **C. Dedicated Instances:** they give hardware isolation, but without visibility into sockets, cores or host placement the company cannot meet socket- or core-based license terms.
- ✗ **D. License-included On-Demand:** this charges for a new license every hour, which is the opposite of reusing the licenses the company already owns.

## Key idea
Reusing licenses counted per socket, per core or per physical server points to EC2 Dedicated Hosts (BYOL).
Q005899:
## EC2 purchasing options at a glance
- **On-Demand**: pay by the second (most Linux and Windows instances) or by the hour, no commitment. Good for short, unpredictable workloads.
- **Savings Plans / Reserved Instances**: commit to one or three years of usage for a lower rate. Good for steady workloads.
- **Spot Instances**: use spare EC2 capacity for up to 90% off On-Demand prices. AWS can reclaim the capacity with a **two-minute interruption notice**.
- **Dedicated Hosts / Dedicated Instances**: hardware not shared with other customers, for compliance or licensing needs, at a higher price.
## When Spot is the right choice
Spot fits work that is **fault-tolerant and flexible**: batch processing, rendering and transcoding, CI builds, big data jobs. If an instance is reclaimed, the job restarts or another instance picks up the work.
## Data transfer is priced separately
Whatever the purchasing option, data transfer has its own prices: data coming into AWS from the internet is free, while data going out to the internet is charged per GB.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reserved Instances:** a one- or three-year commitment suits steady, always-on workloads. A nightly job that can wait gets a bigger discount from Spot without any commitment.
- ✓ **B. Spot Instances (correct):** the job tolerates interruptions and has a flexible deadline, so it can use spare capacity at the deepest discount; if AWS reclaims an instance, the job simply restarts later.
- ✗ **C. On-Demand Instances:** AWS does not reclaim them for capacity, but the company pays the full price for a guarantee the job does not need.
- ✗ **D. Dedicated Hosts:** they cost more than shared capacity and exist for licensing and compliance needs, neither of which the job has.

## Key idea
Interruptible, flexible, fault-tolerant work at the lowest cost points to Spot Instances.
Q005900:
## How Savings Plans work
A Savings Plan is a commitment to spend a fixed amount per hour on compute (for example, `$10/hour`) for one or three years. Usage up to that amount is billed at the lower Savings Plans rate; usage above it is billed On-Demand.
## The two compute plan types
- **Compute Savings Plans**: up to 66% off. Apply to EC2 in **any instance family, size, Region, operating system or tenancy**, and also to **AWS Fargate** and **AWS Lambda**. Most flexible.
- **EC2 Instance Savings Plans**: up to 72% off. Apply to **one instance family in one Region** (size, OS and tenancy can still change). Bigger discount, less flexibility.
## Reserved Instances for comparison
Standard Reserved Instances give a similar discount for a fixed instance configuration in a Region. Convertible Reserved Instances can be exchanged for other EC2 configurations but still cover only EC2, not Fargate or Lambda.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Spot Instances:** Spot is spare EC2 capacity that can be interrupted, which does not suit steady usage, and it is not a discount model for Lambda. (Fargate Spot exists but is a separate, interruptible capacity option.)
- ✗ **B. Standard Reserved Instances:** they are tied to an EC2 configuration in a Region and do not cover Fargate or Lambda, so the planned changes would leave usage at On-Demand rates.
- ✗ **C. EC2 Instance Savings Plans:** the deeper discount is tied to one instance family in one Region, so changing families, moving Regions or shifting to Fargate and Lambda would fall outside the plan.
- ✓ **D. Compute Savings Plans (correct):** the discount follows the company's compute spend across instance families, Regions, Fargate and Lambda, so every planned change stays covered by the commitment.

## Key idea
Steady usage that will change families, Regions or move to Fargate and Lambda points to Compute Savings Plans.
Q005901:
## Resource tags versus cost allocation tags
A tag is a key-value label on a resource, such as `Project=checkout`. Tagging resources alone does not make the tag appear in billing tools. A tag key must also be **activated as a cost allocation tag** in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console (by the management account in an organization).
- **User-defined cost allocation tags**: tags you create, such as `Project` or `CostCenter`.
- **AWS-generated cost allocation tags**: tags AWS adds, such as `aws:createdBy`.
After activation, the tag appears in AWS Cost Explorer as a filter and group-by dimension and as a column in cost and usage data exports. Activation can take up to 24 hours to show up.
## Which tool does what
- **Cost Explorer**: view, filter and forecast past and current costs.
- **AWS Budgets**: set cost or usage thresholds and get alerts.
- **AWS Pricing Calculator**: estimate costs before building.
- **Cost and Usage Report (Data Exports)**: the most detailed line-item billing data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. One Availability Zone per project:** it would distort the architecture for billing reasons, many costs (such as S3 or data transfer) are not tied to one zone, and Cost Explorer can already group by tag once it is activated.
- ✗ **B. Budgets per project:** a budget alerts when spend crosses a threshold, and a budget can be filtered by an active tag, but creating one does not activate the tag or add a dimension to Cost Explorer.
- ✓ **C. Activate the cost allocation tag (correct):** once `Project` is activated as a user-defined cost allocation tag, Cost Explorer can filter and group costs by project, which is exactly the breakdown finance wants.
- ✗ **D. Pricing Calculator:** it produces estimates for planned resources. It cannot report actual monthly charges, and its estimates cannot be uploaded into Cost Explorer.

## Key idea
To break down costs by a tag in Cost Explorer, activate the tag key as a cost allocation tag in the Billing and Cost Management console.
Q005902:
## What consolidated billing is
Consolidated billing is a free feature of AWS Organizations. One account, the **management account**, pays the charges of all **member accounts** in the organization.
## What it gives you
- **One bill**: a single payment method and invoice, while Cost Explorer and the billing data still break costs down by account.
- **Combined usage for volume discounts**: services with tiered pricing (for example, Amazon S3 storage or data transfer) count usage across all accounts, so the organization reaches cheaper tiers sooner.
- **Shared commitment discounts**: Reserved Instance and Savings Plans discounts bought in one account can apply to matching usage in other accounts. Sharing is on by default and can be turned off for specific accounts.
## What it does not do
It does not include a Support plan (Support is per account and paid separately), does not cap spending (use AWS Budgets and budget actions or service control policies for guardrails), and does not merge IAM identities (use IAM Identity Center for single sign-on across accounts).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. One bill, per-account detail (correct):** the management account receives a single invoice for all accounts, while charges stay attributable to each member account.
- ✗ **B. Merged IAM users:** IAM users stay in their own accounts. Single sign-on across accounts is done with IAM Identity Center, not with consolidated billing.
- ✗ **C. Automatic spend caps:** consolidated billing only combines payment. Spending alerts or limits need AWS Budgets, budget actions or other controls.
- ✗ **D. Free Support plan:** Support plans are not included in consolidated billing. Each account's Support plan is purchased separately.
- ✓ **E. Combined usage and shared discounts (correct):** usage is aggregated across accounts for volume pricing tiers, and unused Reserved Instance or Savings Plans discounts can cover usage in other accounts.

## Key idea
Consolidated billing gives one bill, combined volume pricing and shared RI/Savings Plans discounts, at no extra cost.
Q005903:
## AWS Health Dashboard
The AWS Health Dashboard shows the health of AWS services from two angles:
- **Service health**: the public status of AWS services in every Region, visible to anyone.
- **Your account health**: events that affect **your** account and resources, such as scheduled maintenance on specific EC2 instances, required updates, and ongoing service issues, listed with the affected resources.
It is available with every account (including Basic Support). Events can also be sent to Amazon EventBridge to trigger notifications or automation.
## Easily confused tools
- **AWS Trusted Advisor** looks at how you have configured your account (cost, security, fault tolerance, performance, service quotas) and recommends improvements.
- **AWS CloudTrail** records who did what (API activity).
- **AWS Config** records what your resources look like over time and checks them against rules.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config:** it tracks how the team's resources are configured and whether they follow rules. It has no knowledge of AWS-side maintenance or outages.
- ✓ **B. Health Dashboard (correct):** its account view lists AWS events, such as scheduled maintenance and service issues, together with the specific resources in the account they affect, and can notify through EventBridge.
- ✗ **C. CloudTrail:** it logs actions taken through the API by users and services. AWS's maintenance plans and service events are not API calls in the account.
- ✗ **D. Trusted Advisor:** it recommends improvements to the team's own configuration. It does not report AWS maintenance events or AWS service issues.

## Key idea
AWS events that affect your resources (maintenance, service issues) appear in the AWS Health Dashboard; best-practice checks are Trusted Advisor.
Q005904:
## Where to get help and products from outside your team
- **AWS Marketplace**: a digital catalog of third-party software, data and services. You can subscribe with a few clicks, deploy into your account (for example as an AMI, container or SaaS product), and pay through your AWS bill. Many listings offer free trials and pay-as-you-go or contract pricing; some offer private offers negotiated with the seller.
- **AWS Partner Network (APN)**: companies that build on AWS or help customers use it. The **AWS Partner Solutions Finder** helps you find a partner, for example for migration consulting.
- **AWS Professional Services**: AWS's own consultants for large engagements.
- **AWS re:Post**: a community Q&A site with answers from customers, partners and AWS experts, plus Knowledge Center articles.
- **AWS Service Catalog**: your own internal catalog of approved products (often CloudFormation templates) that users can launch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Marketplace (correct):** it is the AWS catalog for buying and deploying third-party software, and its charges are billed through the customer's AWS account, so no separate vendor contract or invoice is needed.
- ✗ **B. Service Catalog:** it distributes products that the company's own administrators have already approved. It is not a place to buy software from outside vendors.
- ✗ **C.:** re:Post: it answers questions about using AWS. It does not sell software or put third-party charges on the AWS bill.
- ✗ **D. Partner Solutions Finder:** it helps locate partners to work with, but engaging a consulting partner usually means a separate agreement, not a software subscription billed through AWS.

## Key idea
Find, subscribe to and pay for third-party software through your AWS bill with AWS Marketplace.
Q005905:
## Stateful versus stateless filtering
A VPC has two built-in packet filters, and they remember traffic differently.
- **Security groups** are **stateful**. When an inbound request is allowed, the response is allowed back out automatically, whatever the outbound rules say.
- **Network ACLs** are **stateless**. Each packet is checked on its own, so the response leaving the subnet must be allowed by an outbound rule just like the request entering it.
## What responses look like
A browser connects from a random high port on the client, called an ephemeral port (for example `52814`), to port `443` on the server. The server's reply goes back to that ephemeral port. A network ACL therefore needs an outbound rule such as "allow TCP `1024-65535` to `0.0.0.0/0`" so replies can leave.
A custom network ACL starts with only its final deny-all rules in both directions, so adding inbound rules alone lets requests in but drops every reply.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Only between subnets:** network ACLs filter all traffic entering and leaving the subnet, including internet traffic. Route tables decide where packets go, not whether they are allowed.
- ✗ **B. Stateless security group:** security groups are stateful, so the response to an allowed inbound request leaves automatically without an outbound rule for it.
- ✓ **C. Stateless network ACL (correct):** the requests reach the instance, but the replies to the clients' ephemeral ports hit the outbound default deny and are dropped, so the subnet needs an outbound allow rule for those ports.
- ✗ **D. Cannot be combined:** network ACLs and security groups always work together as two layers. Traffic must pass both, and neither switches the other off.

## Key idea
Network ACLs are stateless and need explicit rules for return traffic; security groups are stateful and allow responses automatically.
Q005906:
## Security groups can point at other security groups
A security group rule's source does not have to be an IP range. It can be another **security group ID**, such as `sg-0abc1234`. The rule then means "allow traffic from any network interface that belongs to that group".
## Why this suits Auto Scaling
Instances launched by Auto Scaling get new private IP addresses each time. A rule that lists IP addresses goes stale as soon as an instance is replaced. A rule that references the web tier's security group follows membership instead: every new web server that joins the group is allowed, and every terminated one is gone, with no rule changes.
Example: database group rule "TCP `3306`, source `sg-web`". Only instances in `sg-web` can open MySQL connections; nothing else in the VPC can.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Each private IP address:** instance IPs change whenever Auto Scaling replaces servers, so the list would have to be edited constantly and would block new servers until it was.
- ✗ **B. Outbound deny rule:** security groups support only allow rules, so a deny rule cannot be written, and restricting the web tier would not stop other sources from reaching the database.
- ✗ **C. Network ACL deny rules:** a subnet-wide rule cannot tell web servers apart from other instances in the same subnet, and maintaining CIDR-based exceptions is more work than one group reference.
- ✓ **D. Security group as the source (correct):** the rule follows group membership, so every web server Auto Scaling launches is allowed automatically and nothing else can reach port 3306.

## Key idea
Reference a security group as a rule's source to allow traffic from whatever instances are in that group, even as they change.
Q005907:
## Two layers of network filtering in a VPC
- **Where it applies**: a security group is attached to an elastic network interface, so it protects individual resources such as EC2 instances or RDS databases. A network ACL is attached to a subnet and covers everything in it.
- **Rule types**: security groups have allow rules only. Network ACLs have both allow and deny rules.
- **Evaluation**: a security group looks at all its rules together; if any rule allows the traffic, it passes. A network ACL checks numbered rules from the lowest number up and applies the first match.
- **State**: security groups are stateful (responses are allowed automatically); network ACLs are stateless.
Example: to block one attacker IP address while allowing everyone else, you need a network ACL deny rule, because a security group cannot express "deny".

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Explicit deny rules:** deny rules exist only in network ACLs. Security groups cannot deny a specific address.
- ✓ **B. Attached to network interfaces (correct):** security groups work at the resource level through the network interface, which is why two instances in the same subnet can have different rules.
- ✗ **C. Numbered rules, first match:** ordered evaluation by rule number is how network ACLs work. A security group evaluates all its rules together.
- ✗ **D. Associated with subnets:** that describes a network ACL. Security groups are attached to resources, not subnets.
- ✓ **E. Allow rules only (correct):** a security group denies everything by default and opens only what its allow rules list; there is no way to write a deny rule.

## Key idea
Security groups: resource level, allow only, all rules evaluated, stateful. Network ACLs: subnet level, allow and deny, numbered order, stateless.
Q005908:
## Two tiers of AWS Shield
AWS Shield is the AWS service for protection against distributed denial of service (DDoS) attacks.
- **Shield Standard** is always on for every AWS customer at no extra cost. It defends against the most common network and transport layer attacks (layer 3 and 4), such as SYN floods and UDP reflection attacks, for traffic reaching AWS.
- **Shield Advanced** is a paid subscription you turn on for specific resources (for example CloudFront distributions, load balancers, Elastic IP addresses or Route 53 hosted zones). It adds tailored detection and mitigation, attack visibility, access to the Shield Response Team and DDoS cost protection.
## Where AWS WAF fits
AWS WAF works at the application layer (layer 7). It inspects HTTP and HTTPS requests and can block patterns such as SQL injection or floods of requests from one source. It complements Shield; it is not what gives basic DDoS protection.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Shield Standard (correct):** it is included automatically for every AWS customer at no additional charge and mitigates common layer 3 and layer 4 DDoS attacks, so the bookshop already has it.
- ✗ **B. Shield Advanced on by default:** Shield Advanced is a paid subscription that a customer must choose to turn on and assign to resources. It is not enabled automatically.
- ✗ **C. GuardDuty blocks DDoS:** GuardDuty detects threats and reports findings; it does not block traffic, and it is not a DDoS mitigation service.
- ✗ **D. Nothing without WAF:** basic DDoS protection comes from Shield Standard, which is already active. AWS WAF filters web requests at the application layer and must be configured with rules.

## Key idea
Every AWS customer gets Shield Standard automatically at no extra cost; Shield Advanced is the paid tier for extra protection.
Q005909:
## Why DDoS can become a billing problem
Elastic services are designed to absorb load. During a DDoS attack, CloudFront, load balancers and Auto Scaling groups may serve far more requests or add capacity, and that usage is billed like normal traffic.
## DDoS cost protection
**AWS Shield Advanced** includes **DDoS cost protection**: if a protected resource scales up because of a DDoS attack, the customer can request service credits for the related usage charges. Shield Advanced also offers:
- Enhanced detection and mitigation tuned to the protected resources.
- Near real-time visibility and reports about attacks.
- Access to the Shield Response Team for help during an attack.
Shield Standard, the free tier every customer has, mitigates common attacks but does not include cost protection.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Firewall Manager stops scaling:** Firewall Manager centrally applies firewall and protection policies across accounts. It does not control Auto Scaling or decide whether traffic is an attack.
- ✗ **B. AWS Budgets refunds:** Budgets tracks spending and sends alerts (and can run actions such as applying a policy), but it never refunds charges.
- ✗ **C. Shield Standard bill cap:** Shield Standard mitigates common network attacks but includes no billing safeguard, and no AWS feature caps a bill at a past average.
- ✓ **D. Shield Advanced cost protection (correct):** it is the AWS feature designed to give credits for charges caused by attack-driven scaling of protected resources, which is exactly the finance team's concern.

## Key idea
DDoS cost protection (credits for attack-driven scaling) is a Shield Advanced feature, not part of Shield Standard.
Q005910:
## Application layer protection with AWS WAF
AWS WAF is a web application firewall. You create a **web ACL** and attach it to resources such as a CloudFront distribution, an Application Load Balancer or an API Gateway API. The web ACL holds rules that inspect each HTTP or HTTPS request and allow, block or count it.
## Kinds of WAF rules
- **Match rules**: look for patterns such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting, certain headers, or requests from specific countries.
- **Managed rule groups**: ready-made rule sets maintained by AWS or by AWS Marketplace sellers.
- **Rate-based rules**: count requests from each client (for example each IP address) over a time window and act on clients that go over the limit. When the rate drops back below the limit, the block is lifted.
Example: a rate-based rule scoped to `/login` blocks any IP address that sends more requests than the limit within the evaluation window, which stops simple credential-stuffing bots.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Inspector scan of the login page:** Inspector finds software vulnerabilities in EC2 instances, container images and Lambda functions. It does not inspect or block incoming web requests.
- ✗ **B. Network ACL rate limit:** network ACL rules match addresses, protocols and ports only. They have no counters or request-rate limits.
- ✓ **C. WAF rate-based rule (correct):** it tracks request rates per IP address and blocks addresses that exceed the limit, which is exactly the automatic throttling of abusive bots the company wants.
- ✗ **D. Security group connection limit:** security group rules can only allow traffic by protocol, port and source. They cannot limit how many requests a source sends.

## Key idea
To block clients that send too many web requests, use an AWS WAF rate-based rule.
Q005911:
## AWS WAF works on web requests
AWS WAF understands HTTP and HTTPS. It can only be attached to services that receive web requests and can hand them to WAF for inspection. Supported resource types include:
- Amazon CloudFront distributions.
- Application Load Balancers.
- Amazon API Gateway REST APIs.
- AWS AppSync GraphQL APIs and Amazon Cognito user pools, among others.
## What WAF cannot protect directly
Resources that handle raw TCP/UDP connections or are not reached through a web request path, such as Network Load Balancers, NAT gateways or databases, cannot have a web ACL. They are protected with security groups, network ACLs, AWS Network Firewall and AWS Shield instead.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. NAT gateway:** a NAT gateway translates outbound traffic from private subnets. It is not a WAF resource; outbound filtering would use AWS Network Firewall.
- ✓ **B. CloudFront distribution (correct):** CloudFront is a primary WAF integration; rules run at edge locations before requests reach the origin.
- ✗ **C. RDS database instance:** databases are reached over database protocols, not web requests, and are protected with security groups and network placement, not WAF.
- ✗ **D. Network Load Balancer:** an NLB works at layer 4 and passes TCP or UDP connections without parsing HTTP, so AWS WAF cannot be associated with it.
- ✓ **E. Application Load Balancer (correct):** an ALB handles HTTP and HTTPS at layer 7, so a web ACL can inspect each request before it is routed to the targets.

## Key idea
AWS WAF attaches to web-facing resources such as CloudFront, Application Load Balancers and API Gateway, not to Network Load Balancers, NAT gateways or databases.
Q005912:
## Filtering at the VPC boundary
Security groups and network ACLs filter by IP address, protocol and port. Some organizations need more: looking inside traffic for attack signatures, and controlling which internet domains servers may contact.
## AWS Network Firewall
AWS Network Firewall is a managed network firewall that you deploy into a VPC, usually in its own firewall subnet, with route tables sending traffic through it.
- **Stateful inspection** of traffic flows, including traffic to and from the internet, between VPCs and to on-premises networks.
- **Intrusion prevention (IPS)** with rules compatible with the open-source Suricata format, plus AWS managed rule groups.
- **Domain filtering**: allow or deny outbound traffic by domain name, for example only `*.example-updates.com`.
- AWS scales and maintains the firewall infrastructure.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS WAF:** WAF protects web applications from incoming HTTP requests. It does not inspect all VPC traffic or filter the servers' outbound connections by domain.
- ✗ **B. Amazon GuardDuty:** GuardDuty detects threats and creates findings, but it does not sit in the traffic path and cannot block or filter connections.
- ✓ **C. AWS Network Firewall (correct):** it inspects VPC traffic statefully, supports intrusion prevention rules and can restrict outbound connections to an allow list of domains, covering all three requirements.
- ✗ **D. Security groups:** they allow traffic by protocol, port and IP address only. They cannot match domain names or detect intrusion signatures in traffic.

## Key idea
For stateful inspection, intrusion prevention and domain filtering of VPC traffic, use AWS Network Firewall.
Q005913:
## Managing firewalls at organization scale
Setting up WAF rules or security groups one account at a time is slow and easy to get wrong. New accounts and new resources can easily slip through without protection.
## AWS Firewall Manager
AWS Firewall Manager is a security management service for organizations that use **AWS Organizations**. A designated administrator account creates **policies** once, and Firewall Manager applies them across the chosen accounts and resources.
- Supported policy types include AWS WAF rules, AWS Shield Advanced protections, security group policies, AWS Network Firewall and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall.
- New accounts and newly created resources in scope are protected automatically.
- It reports resources that are not compliant with a policy.
Firewall Manager does not inspect traffic itself; it deploys and enforces the services that do.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector finds vulnerabilities and network exposure. It does not create or enforce WAF rules or security group policies.
- ✗ **B. AWS Shield Standard:** it gives automatic baseline DDoS protection, but it has no WAF rules or security group policies to distribute.
- ✗ **C. AWS Network Firewall:** it is a firewall that filters VPC traffic, but each deployment is configured where it runs. Rolling it out consistently across accounts is a job for Firewall Manager.
- ✓ **D. AWS Firewall Manager (correct):** it lets one administrator define WAF and security group policies once and enforces them across all accounts in the organization, including new ones.

## Key idea
To apply WAF, Shield Advanced and security group policies consistently across many accounts, use AWS Firewall Manager with AWS Organizations.
Q005914:
## Vulnerability management
A **CVE** (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures entry) is a publicly listed security flaw in a software package, such as an old OpenSSL version. Images and servers built last month can become vulnerable today when a new CVE is published.
## Amazon Inspector
Amazon Inspector is an automated vulnerability management service.
- **Amazon ECR images**: scanned when pushed and rescanned when new CVEs that affect them are published.
- **Amazon EC2 instances**: checked for software vulnerabilities and unintended network exposure.
- **AWS Lambda functions**: checked for vulnerable packages in the function code and dependencies.
Each finding includes a severity score and remediation guidance, such as the package version that fixes the problem.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Amazon Inspector (correct):** it scans ECR container images on push and continuously rescans them as new CVEs appear, which matches both requirements.
- ✗ **B. AWS Config:** Config checks resource settings against rules, such as whether encryption is on. It does not inspect the software packages inside an image.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Detective:** Detective helps investigate security findings after they happen. It does not scan images for known CVEs.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not look for software vulnerabilities in container images.

## Key idea
Known software vulnerabilities (CVEs) in EC2, container images and Lambda are found by Amazon Inspector.
Q005915:
## Knowing where sensitive data lives
You cannot protect data you do not know about. Large organizations often have old buckets with unknown contents, and auditors ask where personal data is stored.
## Amazon Macie
Amazon Macie is a data security service for Amazon S3.
- It builds an inventory of buckets and evaluates their security, for example whether a bucket is public or unencrypted.
- It runs **sensitive data discovery**: managed data identifiers recognize types such as names, addresses, passport numbers, credit card numbers and credentials, and custom identifiers can match company-specific patterns.
- Findings show which objects contain which kinds of sensitive data, and they can be sent to Security Hub CSPM or Amazon EventBridge.
Example: Macie reports that `claims-archive-2017` holds 4,000 objects containing passport numbers, so the team knows which bucket to lock down first.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon GuardDuty:** GuardDuty looks for threats in how S3 is accessed. It does not read object contents to classify what data is stored.
- ✗ **B. AWS Trusted Advisor:** its S3 check flags buckets with open permissions. It says nothing about whether the objects inside contain personal data.
- ✗ **C. AWS Key Management Service:** KMS protects data with encryption once you decide to use it, but it does not discover which objects contain personal data.
- ✓ **D. Amazon Macie (correct):** it is built to scan S3 objects and identify personally identifiable information, so it shows exactly which buckets hold PII.

## Key idea
To discover personal or sensitive data stored in Amazon S3, use Amazon Macie.
Q005916:
## Detect, then investigate
Security tools do different jobs along an incident:
- **Detect**: Amazon GuardDuty raises a finding, such as unusual API calls by a role.
- **Investigate**: someone must answer "what happened, how far did it go, and is this normal?".
- **Respond**: block, rotate credentials, isolate resources.
## Amazon Detective
Amazon Detective automatically collects data such as AWS CloudTrail events, VPC Flow Logs and GuardDuty findings and organizes it into a **behavior graph** that links identities, IP addresses and resources over time.
- Visualizations show an entity's activity compared with its usual baseline.
- Analysts can pivot from a GuardDuty finding to the role, then to the IP address, and see every related interaction.
- It removes the need to query and join raw logs by hand.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector finds software vulnerabilities. It does not trace what an identity did or where an IP address connected.
- ✓ **B. Amazon Detective (correct):** it links the finding to the role's activity, its baseline and the IP address's other interactions, which is the root cause investigation the analyst needs.
- ✗ **C. AWS Firewall Manager:** blocking the address may be a later response step, but Firewall Manager provides no investigation of the role's behavior.
- ✗ **D. AWS Secrets Manager:** IAM roles use temporary credentials from AWS STS, not secrets stored in Secrets Manager, and rotating secrets does not explain what happened.

## Key idea
GuardDuty detects suspicious activity; Amazon Detective helps investigate its root cause and scope.
Q005917:
## Too many consoles
Each security service produces its own findings in its own console. With several services and several accounts, nobody sees the full picture.
## AWS Security Hub CSPM
AWS Security Hub CSPM (cloud security posture management) gives a central view of security across accounts.
- **Aggregation**: it collects findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, Macie, other AWS services and AWS Partner Network products in a standard format.
- **Security standards**: it runs automated control checks against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices, the CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark and PCI DSS, and gives a security score. These checks rely on AWS Config recording resources.
- **Multi-account**: with AWS Organizations, a delegated administrator account can see every member account.
- **Automation**: findings can trigger responses through Amazon EventBridge.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Security Hub CSPM (correct):** it collects GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings in one place and continuously checks accounts against the AWS Foundational Security Best Practices standard.
- ✗ **B. AWS Trusted Advisor:** it runs its own best-practice checks and can display Security Hub CSPM control results, but it does not aggregate GuardDuty, Inspector and Macie findings or run the standard's checks itself.
- ✗ **C. AWS Artifact:** Artifact provides AWS's own audit reports. It does not check the company's accounts or gather security findings.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Detective:** Detective helps investigate individual findings in depth, but it does not run compliance standard checks or act as the central findings dashboard.

## Key idea
AWS Security Hub CSPM aggregates findings from security services and scores accounts against standards such as AWS Foundational Security Best Practices.
Q005918:
## Match the service to the question
Several AWS security services produce similar-looking findings, so it helps to remember the one question each answers:
- **Amazon Macie**: "Where is sensitive data stored in S3?"
- **Amazon Inspector**: "Which workloads run software with known vulnerabilities?"
- **Amazon GuardDuty**: "Is something malicious happening in my account or network right now?"
- **Amazon Detective**: "What exactly happened around this finding, and how far did it spread?"
- **AWS Security Hub CSPM**: "What is my overall posture across all these services and accounts?"

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Shield Standard:** Shield mitigates DDoS attacks against traffic. It never scans software on instances.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Detective:** Detective investigates findings using log data. It does not read S3 object contents to classify personal data.
- ✓ **C. Amazon Macie (correct):** it inspects S3 objects with managed data identifiers and reports which files contain personal data such as passport numbers.
- ✗ **D. AWS Certificate Manager:** ACM provisions TLS certificates. It has no feature for searching stored data.
- ✓ **E. Amazon Inspector (correct):** it scans EC2 instances for installed packages that match published CVEs and reports each vulnerability with a severity.

## Key idea
Sensitive data in S3 is Amazon Macie; software vulnerabilities in workloads is Amazon Inspector.
Q005919:
## Managing encryption keys
Encryption is only as strong as the control over its keys. Regulated companies typically need to decide who may use a key, to be able to switch a key off, and to prove when it was used.
## AWS KMS
AWS Key Management Service creates and manages cryptographic keys and is integrated with most AWS services that store data, including Amazon S3, Amazon EBS and Amazon RDS.
- Key material is protected by hardware security modules (HSMs) that are validated under FIPS 140 and never leaves KMS unencrypted.
- **Customer managed keys** let you write the key policy, grant or revoke use, enable optional automatic rotation, and disable or schedule deletion of a key.
- Every use of a key, such as `Decrypt` or `GenerateDataKey`, is recorded in **AWS CloudTrail**, which gives the audit trail.
Example: after a customer managed key is disabled, KMS refuses new requests to use it, so the data it protects cannot be decrypted again until the key is re-enabled.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Certificate Manager:** ACM manages TLS certificates for encrypting data in transit. It does not provide the keys that encrypt S3 objects or EBS volumes at rest.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data in S3. It does not control or audit encryption keys.
- ✗ **C. Secrets Manager:** Secrets Manager stores credentials such as database passwords and itself encrypts them with KMS keys. It is not the service that S3 and EBS use for their encryption keys.
- ✓ **D. AWS KMS customer managed keys (correct):** the bank writes the key policy, can disable the key at any time, and every request to use the key is logged in CloudTrail.

## Key idea
To create, control, disable and audit encryption keys used by AWS services, use AWS KMS customer managed keys with CloudTrail logging.
Q005920:
## TLS certificates protect data in transit
HTTPS uses a TLS certificate to prove a website's identity and encrypt the connection. Certificates expire, and an expired certificate makes browsers show warnings, which is a common cause of outages.
## AWS Certificate Manager
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions, manages and deploys TLS certificates.
- **Public certificates** for your domains, after you prove you control the domain (DNS validation is the usual method).
- Deployment to **integrated services** such as Elastic Load Balancing, Amazon CloudFront and Amazon API Gateway with a few clicks.
- **Managed renewal**: ACM renews certificates it issued before they expire, and with DNS validation this needs no manual steps.
Example: a certificate for `booking.example.com` is attached to the ALB's HTTPS listener and is renewed automatically each cycle.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS KMS:** KMS manages encryption keys used for data at rest. It does not issue public TLS certificates for websites.
- ✓ **B. AWS Certificate Manager (correct):** it issues the public TLS certificate, attaches it to the Application Load Balancer and renews it automatically, so nobody has to track expiry dates.
- ✗ **C. AWS Shield Advanced:** Shield Advanced protects against DDoS attacks. It does not provide or renew TLS certificates.
- ✗ **D. AWS Secrets Manager:** Secrets Manager stores secrets such as passwords and API keys. It does not issue public certificates or deploy them to load balancers.

## Key idea
Public TLS certificates for load balancers, CloudFront and API Gateway, with automatic renewal, come from AWS Certificate Manager.
Q005921:
## Why hard-coded passwords are risky
A password in a configuration file is copied to every clone of the repository, may end up in logs or backups, and rarely gets changed because changing it means redeploying code.
## AWS Secrets Manager
AWS Secrets Manager stores secrets such as database credentials, API keys and tokens.
- Secrets are encrypted at rest with AWS KMS keys.
- Applications fetch the secret at runtime with an API call such as `GetSecretValue`, and IAM policies decide who may read it.
- **Automatic rotation**: Secrets Manager can change credentials on a schedule, with managed rotation for databases such as Amazon RDS or a Lambda function for other secrets, and the application always reads the current value.
- Access is logged in AWS CloudTrail.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. AWS Secrets Manager (correct):** it removes the password from the code, lets the application retrieve it at runtime under IAM control, and rotates database credentials automatically.
- ✗ **B. AWS Certificate Manager:** ACM manages TLS certificates. It does not store passwords, and certificate renewal has nothing to do with database credentials.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data in Amazon S3. It does not scan code repositories or rewrite configuration files.
- ✗ **D. AWS KMS:** KMS manages encryption keys, not application passwords. Its key rotation changes key material and does not change a database password.

## Key idea
Store, retrieve and automatically rotate application secrets such as database passwords with AWS Secrets Manager.
Q005922:
## Best-practice checks for your account
AWS Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and makes recommendations in categories including cost optimization, performance, fault tolerance, service limits (quotas), operational excellence and **security**.
## Typical security checks
- Security groups that allow unrestricted access (`0.0.0.0/0`) to specific ports such as SSH or RDP.
- Multi-factor authentication (MFA) not enabled on the root user.
- Amazon S3 buckets with open access permissions.
- Publicly shared Amazon EBS or Amazon RDS snapshots.
Each check shows a status (green, yellow or red), the affected resources and a recommended action. A core set of security checks is available to every account; how many checks you see depends on your support plan.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Health Dashboard:** it reports AWS events that affect your resources, such as service issues and maintenance, not misconfigurations in your account.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector looks for software vulnerabilities in workloads. It does not check root user MFA settings.
- ✓ **C. AWS Trusted Advisor (correct):** its security checks look at the account's own configuration and flag issues such as unrestricted security group ports and a root user without MFA, with recommended fixes.
- ✗ **D. AWS Artifact:** Artifact provides AWS's compliance reports about its own infrastructure. It does not inspect the customer's account configuration.

## Key idea
AWS Trusted Advisor security checks flag common account misconfigurations, such as open security group ports and no MFA on the root user.
Q005923:

AWS publishes several free resources for solving problems and learning best practices without contacting AWS Support:

- **AWS documentation**: service user guides and API references.
- **AWS Security Blog and AWS security pages**: security guidance, new features and security bulletins.

## Why each option works or fails

For AWS-written answers to common troubleshooting questions, check the AWS Knowledge Center on AWS re:Post.
Q005924:
## Where AWS publishes security information
Not every security resource is a service you turn on. AWS also publishes information that every customer can read:

For AWS security bulletins and expert guidance, follow the AWS security website (Security Center) and the AWS Security Blog.
Q005925:
## AWS Marketplace for security
AWS Marketplace is a curated digital catalog where customers find, buy and deploy software from independent vendors. Its security category includes firewalls, endpoint protection, vulnerability management, identity, and SIEM (security information and event management) products.
- Products can be delivered as Amazon Machine Images (AMIs), containers, SaaS subscriptions and other formats.

AWS-native controls such as security groups keep working alongside it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Requires a support plan:** subscribing to Marketplace products does not depend on the customer's AWS Support plan.
- ✓ **B. Security products in Marketplace (correct):** AWS Marketplace has a large security category where customers can find firewall, endpoint protection and SIEM products from AWS Partners, often the same vendors they use on premises.
- ✗ **C. Replaces security groups:** a third-party firewall adds another layer. Security groups cannot be switched off and keep filtering traffic to each resource.
- ✗ **D. AWS takes over responsibility:** AWS Marketplace is a catalog and billing channel. AWS does not manage the rules or patches of third-party software in a customer's account.
- ✓ **E. Customer still operates it (correct):** software deployed in the customer's account is customer-managed, so the hospital configures the firewall's rules and keeps it updated.

## Key idea
AWS Marketplace offers third-party security products, but the customer still configures and operates whatever it deploys.
Q005926:
## Three levels of machine learning on AWS
AWS offers ML at different levels of effort and control:
- **Pre-trained AI services** (Rekognition, Comprehend, Textract, Transcribe and others): call an API, no model building. Each solves one common task.
- **Generative AI with foundation models** (Amazon Bedrock): use large models that someone else trained, through one API, and adapt them with prompts, retrieval or fine-tuning.
- **Build your own model** (Amazon SageMaker AI): your data scientists choose the algorithm, train on your data and deploy the result.
## What SageMaker AI manages for you
- Notebooks for exploring data and writing training code.
- Training jobs that start compute, run the training and shut the compute down when finished.
- Automatic model tuning to try many hyperparameter combinations.
- Hosted endpoints that serve predictions to applications, with scaling handled by the service.
## Example
The team trains a model on five years of shipments (route, weather, carrier, warehouse) to predict `late = yes/no`, then deploys it to an endpoint the routing application calls for each new shipment.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Comprehend:** it analyzes text with models AWS has already trained. It cannot be used to train a delivery-delay predictor on the company's own numeric shipment data.
- ✗ **B. Amazon EMR:** it runs big data processing clusters. It could prepare the data, but it does not provide the managed training, tuning and model hosting the team asked for.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Bedrock:** it serves pre-trained foundation models for generative AI tasks such as text and image generation. It is not the tool for training a tabular prediction model from scratch on shipment records.
- ✓ **D. SageMaker AI (correct):** it is the managed service for the full custom-model lifecycle, from notebooks and training jobs to tuning and hosted inference endpoints, without the team running servers.

## Key idea
Build, train and deploy your own ML model without managing servers = Amazon SageMaker AI.
Q005927:
## Generative AI and foundation models
A **foundation model (FM)** is a very large model trained on huge amounts of data. It can summarize, answer questions, write drafts and more, guided by a text **prompt**. Training one costs far too much for most companies, so they use existing models.
## Amazon Bedrock
- One API gives access to models from Amazon (such as Amazon Nova) and other providers (such as Anthropic, Meta and Mistral AI), so a team can compare models and switch between them.
- Serverless: no instances or GPUs to manage. You pay for what you use, for example per input and output token.
- Models can be adapted with your own data, for example through **Knowledge Bases** (retrieval-augmented generation over your documents) or fine-tuning.
- Your prompts and data are not used to train the providers' base models.
## Where the other services fit
- **SageMaker AI**: build and train your own models.
- **Lex**: intent-based chatbots.
- **Textract**: get the text out of a scanned document; a Bedrock model could then summarize it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Lex:** it matches what a user says to predefined intents and collects details. It does not write summaries of long free-text notes.
- ✓ **B. Amazon Bedrock (correct):** it provides foundation models from several providers behind one serverless API, priced by use, so the company can add summarization and question answering without training models or running infrastructure.
- ✗ **C. SageMaker AI:** it is aimed at teams that build and train their own models. The company explicitly does not want to train or host a model itself.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Textract:** it extracts text and structure from scanned pages. It can feed the notes into a summarizer but cannot write summaries or answer questions.

## Key idea
Generative AI from multiple foundation models through one serverless API = Amazon Bedrock.
Q005928:
## From paper to data
Optical character recognition (OCR) turns an image of text into characters. Plain OCR, however, returns lines of words without knowing what they mean. **Amazon Textract** goes further:
- **Forms**: it returns key-value pairs, for example `Applicant name: Jane Park`.
- **Tables**: it keeps rows and columns, so an income table stays a table.
- **Handwriting**: it reads handwritten as well as printed text.
- **Queries**: you can ask for a specific field, such as "What is the annual income?"
There is no model to train. You send a document image or PDF and get structured results back.
## Example pipeline
A scanned form lands in Amazon S3, a Lambda function calls Textract, and the extracted fields are written to the loan system. Comprehend could then analyze any free-text comments if needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Comprehend:** it works on text that already exists as characters. It cannot read a scanned image, so the forms would first need extraction.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Transcribe:** it converts spoken audio into text. Loan forms are images, not recordings.
- ✓ **C. Amazon Textract (correct):** it is built to read scanned forms, returning field names with their values and table cells in structure, which removes the manual retyping.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Rekognition:** it analyzes images for objects, faces and scenes. It can spot short text in a photo, but it does not understand forms or keep table structure.

## Key idea
Text, forms and tables from scanned documents = Amazon Textract.
Q005929:
## Computer vision as an API
Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and videos with models AWS has trained. Common uses:
- **Labels**: objects and scenes, such as `car`, `beach`, `dog`.
- **Face analysis and comparison**: detect faces, and compare a face in a source image with faces in a target image to get a similarity score.
- **Face liveness**: check that a real person is in front of the camera rather than a printed photo.
- **Content moderation**: flag images that contain unsafe or inappropriate content.
- **Custom labels**: train it on your own image categories with a small labeled set.
## Combining services
Identity checks often use two services together: Rekognition compares the faces, and Textract reads the text fields on the ID document. The question asks only about matching the faces.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Comprehend:** it finds personal information in text. It does not analyze images or faces.
- ✗ **B. SageMaker AI:** a custom model is possible but would require collecting and labeling data and training, which the company wants to avoid when a ready-made API exists.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Textract:** it is useful for reading the printed fields on the licence, but it does not compare faces between two images.
- ✓ **D. Amazon Rekognition (correct):** its face comparison feature takes the selfie and the licence photo and returns how similar the faces are, so the app can verify the driver with no ML development.

## Key idea
Faces, objects and unsafe content in images and video = Amazon Rekognition.
Q005930:
## Natural language processing (NLP)
NLP lets software find meaning in human language. **Amazon Comprehend** is a managed NLP service with pre-trained models:
- **Sentiment**: positive, negative, neutral or mixed.
- **Key phrases**: the main talking points, such as "slow check-in" or "breakfast buffet".
- **Entities**: people, places, organizations, dates, quantities.
- **Language detection** and **PII detection** (finding personal data such as phone numbers).
- **Custom classification**: train it to sort text into your own categories, such as complaint types.
## Example

## Two ways to handle streaming data
- **Amazon Kinesis Data Streams**: a durable stream you read with your own consumers (for example Lambda or applications on EC2). It suits custom real-time processing, where you decide what each consumer does.
- **Amazon Data Firehose** (formerly Kinesis Data Firehose): a fully managed **delivery** service. Producers send records, Firehose buffers them for a short time (seconds to minutes) and writes them to a destination.
## What Firehose can do on the way
- Destinations include Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, Splunk and HTTP endpoints.
- It can convert JSON records to Apache Parquet or Apache ORC before writing to S3, using a table schema from the AWS Glue Data Catalog. Columnar files make later Athena queries faster and cheaper.
- It can compress data and transform records with a Lambda function.
- It scales automatically; there are no shards or consumers to manage.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Glue crawlers:** they catalog data after it has landed in S3. They do not ingest or deliver a live stream of events.
- ✓ **B. Amazon Data Firehose (correct):** it is the managed way to load streaming data into S3 in near real time, and it can convert records to a columnar format, with no consumer code or capacity to manage.
- ✗ **C. Amazon SQS:** it is a message queue for decoupling application components, not a delivery service that batches, converts and writes streaming data to S3.
- ✗ **D. Kinesis Data Streams:** it captures the stream, but the team would have to write and run consumer applications to convert the records and write them to S3.

## Key idea
Load streaming data into S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with no code = Amazon Data Firehose; custom stream processing = Kinesis Data Streams.
Q005934:
## OLTP versus OLAP
- **OLTP (online transaction processing)**: many small reads and writes, such as placing an order or updating a stock count. Relational databases like Amazon RDS and Aurora, or DynamoDB, serve this.
- **OLAP (online analytical processing)**: fewer but very large queries that scan millions or billions of rows, such as "sales by region by month for ten years". This is the job of a **data warehouse**.
## Amazon Redshift
- Stores data in **columns**, so a query that needs three columns reads only those three.
- Spreads each query across many nodes in parallel.
- Available as provisioned clusters or **Redshift Serverless**, which scales capacity automatically.
- Can also query data in S3 (Redshift Spectrum) and connect to BI tools such as Amazon Quick Sight.
## When Athena is enough
For occasional queries on files in S3, Athena is simpler. For a central warehouse queried heavily all day by many users, Redshift is the usual choice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon DynamoDB:** it excels at fast lookups by key, but it is not designed for ad hoc SQL joins and aggregations across large data sets.
- ✗ **B. RDS for MySQL:** it is optimized for transactional workloads. Large analytical scans and joins over ten years of data from many systems would be slow and would compete with transactions.
- ✓ **C. Amazon Redshift (correct):** it is AWS's data warehouse, built with columnar storage and parallel processing for frequent, complex analytical SQL across years of data from many sources.
- ✗ **D. OpenSearch Service:** it is strong at text search and log exploration, not at being the central relational warehouse for complex SQL joins over business data.

## Key idea
Central data warehouse for heavy analytical SQL and BI = Amazon Redshift.
Q005935:
## AWS Glue in two parts
- **Data Catalog**: a central list of databases and tables that describes where data lives and what its columns and types are. Athena, Redshift Spectrum and EMR can all use it, so a table is defined once and used by many tools.
- **Crawlers**: point one at an S3 path and it reads sample files, infers the schema (for example `order_id: string, amount: double`) and creates or updates catalog tables.
- **ETL jobs**: serverless Spark or Python jobs that clean, join and convert data, for example from CSV to Parquet. You pay while the job runs.
## Glue versus EMR
Both can run Spark. **Glue** is serverless and focused on cataloging and ETL. **EMR** gives you clusters of many open-source frameworks (Spark, Hive, HBase, Presto and more) with more control over configuration, often chosen to move existing Hadoop workloads.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Data Firehose:** it delivers incoming streams to S3. It does not discover the schemas of files that are already stored.
- ✗ **B. Amazon Athena:** it queries the files once tables exist, but it relies on a catalog such as the Glue Data Catalog for those definitions and does not run cleaning jobs.
- ✓ **C. AWS Glue (correct):** its crawlers discover the schemas of the files and store them in the Data Catalog, and its serverless ETL jobs clean the data, which covers every requirement.
- ✗ **D. Amazon EMR:** it can transform data, but the team must size and configure clusters, and it does not crawl S3 to build a central schema catalog by itself.

## Key idea
Discover schemas into a central catalog and run serverless ETL = AWS Glue.
Q005936:
## Search is not the same as SQL

- Full-text search with relevance ranking, fuzzy matching for typos, autocomplete and faceted filters (brand, price range).

- ✗ **B. Amazon Redshift:** it is built for analytical SQL over business data, not for relevance-ranked, typo-tolerant keyword search on a website.
- ✗ **C. Amazon Comprehend:** it extracts meaning from text but does not index a catalog or return ranked search results.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Athena:** it answers SQL queries over files in S3 for analysis. It has no relevance scoring and is not designed for per-keystroke shopper searches.

## Key idea
Full-text search and log analytics with a managed engine = Amazon OpenSearch Service.
Q005937:

Fine-grained data lake permissions = AWS Lake Formation; BI dashboards = Amazon Quick Sight.
Q005938:
## Publish/subscribe (pub/sub)
In pub/sub, a sender **publishes** a message to a **topic** and does not need to know who will receive it. Every **subscriber** to the topic gets its own copy.
## Amazon SNS
- Subscriber types include Amazon SQS queues, AWS Lambda functions, HTTP/S endpoints, email addresses, SMS numbers and mobile push.
- Delivery is push-based and immediate.
- **Fan-out**: one SNS topic with several SQS queues subscribed, so different services each process the same event at their own pace.
## Example
The payment service publishes `{"event":"payment_failed","customer":"C-1022"}` to the `payment-alerts` topic. Finance gets an email, the on-call engineer gets an SMS, and the retry queue receives a copy for the retry service.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon SES:** it sends email, but it does not send SMS or deliver messages to an SQS queue.
- ✗ **B. Amazon SQS:** a queue delivers each message to one consumer and cannot send email or SMS, so it covers only the retry part.
- ✗ **C. Step Functions:** it orchestrates a series of tasks. It could call other services in turn, but it is not the simple broadcast mechanism to many subscribers that the requirement describes.
- ✓ **D. Amazon SNS (correct):** one publish to a topic is delivered to every subscriber, and it supports email, SMS and SQS subscriptions, which covers all three destinations.

## Key idea
One message pushed to many subscribers (email, SMS, queues, Lambda) = Amazon SNS.
Q005939:
## Event-driven architecture
An **event** is a record that something happened: an instance stopped, a file was uploaded, an order was placed. Event-driven systems react to events instead of checking repeatedly.
## Amazon EventBridge
- Receives events from AWS services (for example `EC2 Instance State-change Notification`), from your own applications and from supported SaaS partners.
- **Rules** match events by pattern, such as `"state": "stopped"`, and send them to **targets** such as Lambda, SQS, SNS or Step Functions.
- **Schedules** (EventBridge Scheduler or scheduled rules) run targets at fixed times, such as a cron expression for weekdays at 07:00.
- Serverless: nothing to run or patch.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS AppSync:** it builds GraphQL APIs for applications. It does not react to EC2 state changes or run scheduled jobs.
- ✓ **B. Amazon EventBridge (correct):** a rule can match the EC2 state-change event and invoke the first function, and a schedule can invoke the second at 07:00 on weekdays, all without servers.
- ✗ **C. AWS Config:** it tracks configuration and compliance of resources. It does not run code on a schedule or route state-change events to functions.
- ✗ **D. AWS CloudTrail:** it records the API activity behind a stop, but it is a logging and audit service; routing events to a Lambda function is done by EventBridge.

## Key idea
React to events with rules, or run things on a schedule, serverlessly = Amazon EventBridge.
Q005940:
## Orchestration versus messaging
- **Messaging** (SQS, SNS, EventBridge) moves a message or event from one place to another. Each component decides what to do next by itself.
- **Orchestration** keeps the whole process in one place: which step runs first, what happens on failure, and when the process is finished.
## AWS Step Functions
- You define a **state machine**: a set of steps (Lambda functions, AWS service calls, waits, choices, parallel branches).
- Built-in **retry** and **catch** rules handle errors without extra code.
- Standard workflows can run for up to a year and can pause for a callback, for example until an underwriter approves.
- The console shows each execution as a graph, with the status of every step.
## Example
`CheckCredit` -> `VerifyDocuments` -> `WaitForUnderwriter` (callback) -> `Choice: approved?` -> `NotifyCustomer`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon SNS:** it broadcasts messages. It could notify the customer at the end but cannot coordinate the earlier steps.
- ✗ **B. Amazon SQS:** a queue decouples two components but does not know the order of steps, track a loan's overall progress or wait for an approval.
- ✗ **C. Amazon EventBridge:** it routes single events by rules. It does not keep the state of a multi-step process or show it as a diagram.
- ✓ **D. Step Functions (correct):** it coordinates the ordered steps, retries failures automatically, can wait days for a human decision, and shows each loan's progress as a visual workflow.

## Key idea
Coordinate multi-step workflows with retries, waits and visual tracking = AWS Step Functions.
Q005941:
## What Amazon CloudWatch does
CloudWatch is AWS's monitoring service for resources and applications:

- **Logs**: CloudWatch Logs stores log lines from EC2 (through the CloudWatch agent), Lambda, containers and more, and lets you search them.

- **AWS Config**: records resource configuration and checks it against rules.

- ✗ **C. Request tracing:** following a request across services to find slow components is the job of AWS X-Ray.
- ✗ **D. API call history:** recording who did what in the account is the job of AWS CloudTrail, not CloudWatch.
- ✓ **E. CloudWatch Logs (correct):** the CloudWatch agent sends log files from the instances to CloudWatch Logs, where they are stored centrally and can be searched.

Metrics, logs, alarms and dashboards = CloudWatch; API activity = CloudTrail; request traces = X-Ray; configuration rules = Config.

## Connecting devices to the cloud

Securely connect IoT devices over MQTT and route their messages = AWS IoT Core.
Q005948:
## Tasks only the root user can do
The root user is meant to be locked away, but AWS keeps a short list of tasks that require it. Well-known examples:
- Changing the root user's own password or other root credentials.
- Editing or deleting an Amazon S3 bucket policy that was misconfigured to deny all principals.
- Restoring IAM permissions when the only IAM administrator has accidentally removed their own access.
## Why IAM administrators are stuck
In a bucket policy, an explicit `Deny` with `"Principal": "*"` applies to every IAM user and role in the account, including ones with `AdministratorAccess`. An explicit deny always beats any allow, so no IAM identity can fix it. The root user is the documented way back in. (In AWS Organizations, the management account can also run this privileged root task on a member account when centralized root access is turned on.)
Example: a policy meant to deny `s3:DeleteObject` to everyone is written as `"Action": "s3:*"`. The fix is to sign in as root, delete the policy and write a correct one.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Support removes it:** AWS Support does not change customer resource policies for you; the account owner recovers access through the root user.
- ✓ **B. Root user deletes the policy (correct):** removing a bucket policy that denies all principals is one of the documented root-only tasks, because no IAM identity can get past that explicit deny.
- ✗ **C. AdministratorAccess overrides the deny:** an explicit deny in a bucket policy wins over any allow, including allows in AdministratorAccess, so another admin is blocked the same way.
- ✗ **D. Policy expires after 24 hours:** bucket policies have no expiry. The deny stays in place until someone with enough authority removes it.

## Key idea
A bucket policy that denies all principals can be fixed only by the root user, one of the few tasks reserved for it.
Q005949:
## What MFA adds
Multi-factor authentication means a sign-in needs something you know (the password) plus something you have (a device). A stolen password alone is no longer enough.
## MFA types AWS supports for IAM users and the root user
- **Passkeys and security keys** (FIDO2/WebAuthn): a hardware key such as a YubiKey, or a passkey built into a phone or laptop and unlocked with a fingerprint, face or PIN. These resist phishing because they are bound to the real AWS sign-in site.
- **Virtual authenticator apps**: smartphone apps such as Google Authenticator that generate time-based one-time passwords (TOTP).
- **Hardware TOTP tokens**: small physical devices that show a changing six-digit code.
## What is not supported
AWS no longer offers SMS-based MFA for IAM users, and there is no email-link or voice-call MFA option.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Email sign-in link:** email is not an MFA factor in IAM; a compromised mailbox would otherwise defeat the second factor.
- ✗ **B. SMS text codes:** AWS ended SMS-based MFA for IAM users, so text messages are not a supported MFA type.
- ✗ **C. Voice call codes:** IAM has no voice-call MFA; the supported types are passkeys or security keys, authenticator apps and hardware TOTP tokens.
- ✓ **D. Virtual authenticator app (correct):** TOTP apps on a phone are a supported and very common MFA type for IAM users and the root user.
- ✓ **E. FIDO2 security key or passkey (correct):** AWS supports FIDO2 security keys and passkeys, which are also the most phishing-resistant choice.

## Key idea
IAM MFA works with passkeys or FIDO2 security keys, virtual authenticator apps and hardware TOTP tokens, not SMS, email or voice calls.
Q005950:
## Two places to write permissions
AWS lets you grant access from two directions:
- **Identity-based policies** are attached to an IAM user, group or role. They answer "what can this identity do?" Example: a role may `s3:GetObject` on `arn:aws:s3:::invoices/*`.
- **Resource-based policies** are attached to a resource. They answer "who can use this resource?" and must include a `Principal` element naming the account, user, role or service allowed in.
## Common resource-based policies
- Amazon S3 bucket policies
- AWS KMS key policies
- Amazon SQS queue policies and Amazon SNS topic policies
- AWS Lambda function resource policies and IAM role trust policies
Resource-based policies are especially useful for cross-account access, because the resource owner can name a principal from another account directly.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Organizations limit on accounts:** that is a service control policy (SCP), a guardrail that caps permissions in member accounts and grants nothing by itself.
- ✗ **B. Firewall rules on a network interface:** that describes a security group, which filters network traffic rather than authorizing API actions.
- ✓ **C. Attached to a resource and names principals (correct):** that is the definition of a resource-based policy; an S3 bucket policy is the best-known example, and its `Principal` element states who is allowed in.
- ✗ **D. Attached to a user, group or role:** that describes an identity-based policy, the other half of IAM permissions.

## Key idea
Identity-based policies attach to users, groups and roles; resource-based policies attach to a resource and name the principals that may use it.
Q005951:
## Cross-account access with roles
An IAM role has two policies:
- A **trust policy** says who may assume the role, for example the AWS account `111122223333`.
- A **permissions policy** says what the role can do once assumed, for example the AWS managed `ReadOnlyAccess` or `SecurityAudit` policy.
When an auditor in the trusted account assumes the role, AWS Security Token Service (STS) returns **temporary credentials** that expire after a set time (one hour by default). No password or access key from the insurer's account ever leaves it.
## Ending access
To end the engagement, delete the role or remove the audit firm's account from the trust policy. Every action the auditors take is recorded in AWS CloudTrail with the role session name, so activity stays traceable.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Shared root credentials:** the root user has unrestricted access, so sharing it gives auditors far more than read-only and destroys accountability.
- ✓ **B. Cross-account read-only role (correct):** the audit firm's identities assume the role and receive short-lived credentials, the permissions policy keeps them read-only, and access ends cleanly when the role is removed.
- ✗ **C. Public resources:** making data public lets anyone on the internet read it, not just the auditors, and is a serious exposure for an insurer.
- ✗ **D. IAM users with emailed keys:** these are long-term credentials, exactly what the insurer wanted to avoid, and sending them by email adds a leak risk.

## Key idea
For cross-account access, create a role the other account can assume; it hands out temporary credentials scoped by the role's permissions.
Q005952:
## Long-term versus temporary credentials
- **Long-term**: an IAM user's password or access keys. They stay valid until someone rotates or deletes them.
- **Temporary**: issued for a session and expire on their own, typically after minutes to hours.
## AWS STS
AWS Security Token Service is the service behind every role session. Calls such as `AssumeRole` (cross-account and service roles), `AssumeRoleWithSAML` and `AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity` (federation) return three values:
- an access key ID
- a secret access key
- a session token
The AWS SDKs and CLI use them like normal keys until they expire, then request new ones. EC2 instance roles, Lambda execution roles and IAM Identity Center sign-ins all rely on STS under the hood.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. AWS Certificate Manager:** ACM issues TLS certificates for websites and load balancers; AWS API authentication does not use them.
- ✗ **B. AWS KMS:** KMS creates and manages encryption keys for data; it does not issue the credentials used to sign AWS API requests.
- ✗ **C. AWS Secrets Manager:** Secrets Manager stores application secrets such as database passwords. Roles have no stored access keys to hand out.
- ✓ **D. AWS STS (correct):** it issues the temporary access key, secret key and session token that a role session uses, and they expire automatically.

## Key idea
AWS STS is the service that issues temporary credentials whenever a role is assumed or a user is federated.
Q005953:
## Least privilege in practice
Least privilege means granting only the permissions a task needs. In real projects, teams often start broad because they do not yet know what will be needed, then tighten later. The hard part is knowing which actions are really used.
## IAM Access Analyzer policy generation
IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from activity:
- You pick an IAM user or role, a CloudTrail trail and a time range (for example the last 90 days).
- Access Analyzer reads the logged API calls and drafts a policy listing the services and actions used.
- You review it, add resource ARNs where needed, and replace the broad policy with it.
The other Access Analyzer features also support least privilege: external access findings, unused access findings and policy validation checks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. IAM Access Analyzer policy generation (correct):** it builds a draft policy from the role's real activity recorded in CloudTrail, which is exactly the input needed to shrink broad permissions to what is used.
- ✗ **B. Trusted Advisor rewriting policies:** Trusted Advisor runs best-practice checks and recommendations; it does not analyze a role's API activity or rewrite IAM policies.
- ✗ **C. Config conformance packs:** conformance packs bundle AWS Config rules to evaluate compliance; they report on resources but do not author least-privilege policies for a role.
- ✗ **D. Amazon Inspector:** Inspector finds software vulnerabilities and network exposure in EC2, container images and Lambda code, not unused IAM permissions.

## Key idea
To shrink broad permissions, let IAM Access Analyzer generate a policy from the actions recorded in CloudTrail, then review and apply it.
Q005954:
## Zone of trust
When you create an external access analyzer in IAM Access Analyzer, you choose a **zone of trust**: either your account or your whole AWS Organization. Any access granted to a principal outside that zone is "external".
## How it works
Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to read resource-based policies and work out who can reach each resource. It then creates a finding for every resource shared outside the zone, for example:
- an S3 bucket policy that allows another account or the public
- an IAM role trust policy that lets an outside account assume the role
- a KMS key policy, Lambda function policy, SQS queue policy or Secrets Manager secret policy that grants outside access
The team then archives findings for intended sharing and fixes the rest.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Amazon Macie:** Macie discovers sensitive data such as personal information in S3 and reports bucket security posture; it does not analyze role trust policies or KMS key policies.
- ✗ **B. AWS Artifact:** Artifact provides AWS compliance reports and agreements about AWS itself, not information on who can access your resources.
- ✓ **C. Access Analyzer external access findings (correct):** they analyze resource-based policies on buckets, keys, roles and other resource types and report each one that grants access outside the chosen zone of trust.
- ✗ **D. IAM credential report:** the credential report lists IAM users and the status of their passwords, access keys and MFA; it does not cover resource policies or outside accounts.

## Key idea
IAM Access Analyzer finds resources whose policies share access outside your account or organization.
Q005955:
## The IAM credential report
The credential report is an account-level CSV file you can generate from the IAM console, CLI or API. It has one row for each IAM user (plus one for the root user) with columns such as:
- `password_enabled`, `password_last_used`, `password_last_changed`
- `mfa_active`
- `access_key_1_active`, `access_key_1_last_rotated`, `access_key_1_last_used_date` (and the same for key 2)
## What it is good for
Auditors and security teams use it to spot users without MFA, passwords nobody has used for months, and access keys that are old or unused. It is a point-in-time snapshot of IAM users, so it does not cover roles or resource policies; IAM Access Analyzer covers those.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. CloudTrail event history by hand:** CloudTrail records actions, not the current status of each user's credentials, and building the list manually is slow and incomplete.
- ✗ **B. Amazon GuardDuty:** GuardDuty detects threats such as unusual API calls; it is not an inventory of IAM users and their credential status.
- ✓ **C. IAM credential report (correct):** one download gives every IAM user's password, access key rotation and last-used dates and MFA status, which is exactly what the auditor asked for.
- ✗ **D. Trusted Advisor cost check:** cost optimization checks look at idle or underused resources, not at IAM user credentials.

## Key idea
For a quick audit of IAM users' passwords, access keys and MFA, generate the IAM credential report.
Q005956:
## IAM account password policy
Each AWS account has one password policy that applies to its **IAM users**. Settings include:
- minimum length and required character types (upper case, lower case, numbers, symbols)
- password expiration after a set number of days
- preventing reuse of a number of previous passwords
- whether users may change their own password, and whether an expired password needs an administrator reset
Most settings take effect the next time a user changes a password; some, such as expiration, apply right away.
## What it does not cover
- The **root user** password is not governed by the IAM password policy.
- Users in IAM Identity Center or an external identity provider follow that directory's own password rules.
## Checking versus enforcing
The AWS Config managed rule `iam-password-policy` can report whether the account's password policy meets your standard, but it is the password policy itself that enforces the rules when users set passwords.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Config rule blocks weak passwords:** AWS Config evaluates and reports compliance; its password rule checks the account's policy settings but cannot stop a user from picking a password.
- ✗ **B. Secrets Manager rotation per user:** Secrets Manager rotates application secrets such as database credentials; it has no built-in rotation for IAM console passwords and cannot enforce length, character or reuse rules on passwords users choose.
- ✗ **C. SCP with password rules:** service control policies limit which API actions accounts may use; they have no settings for password length or complexity.
- ✓ **D. IAM account password policy (correct):** it is the built-in setting that enforces length, character, expiration and reuse rules whenever IAM users set passwords.

## Key idea
Enforce IAM user password rules with the account password policy; it does not apply to the root user.
